1.1.text: Welcome to JobDiva ATS Mastery. In this lesson, we introduce the Applicant Tracking System, or ATS — software that simplifies sourcing candidates and managing job orders. JobDiva is the ATS used company-wide at HonorVet Technologies, though other platforms like CEIPAL and Bullhorn exist across the staffing industry, and some companies even build their own in-house systems.

What matters most as you get started is understanding that JobDiva uses role-based access: a SuperAdmin or Admin controls the entire system — creating users, configuring settings, and making organization-wide changes — while recruiters see only the portion relevant to their own work. This isn't a limitation to work around; it's intentional. Every user, from a brand-new recruiter to a senior account manager, receives individual login credentials, and those credentials are always provisioned by the SuperAdmin or coordinated through your manager — you'll never set up your own account from scratch. Notice this sign-in screen uses Azure single sign-on with your company email, not a separate JobDiva password.

So if your screen looks different from a colleague's, or you don't see an icon someone else has, that's expected: your JobDiva view is calibrated specifically to your role and responsibilities within the organization, and it will grow as your role does. Take a moment to look at this apps menu — notice the color-coded bars for Sourcing, Jobs, Analytics, and Engagement down the left edge; we'll explore each in detail later in this course.

1.2.text: Let's tour the upper bar of the JobDiva interface, starting with the universal search bar — the tool you'll click into constantly throughout your day. You can search by candidate name, email, phone number, or Job ID and Reference ID, and JobDiva will also surface close matches, so even a partial or slightly-off search term can still return something useful. Notice the 'Include close matches' option right here — checking it widens your results when you're not entirely sure of the exact spelling or number. For the fastest, most precise search, though, use an exact Job ID, Reference ID, or email rather than a generic name, since names can be shared across many candidates, and a broad name search can bury the one record you actually need under dozens of similar ones. Get comfortable with this bar early — it's the fastest path to any candidate or job record once you know its exact identifier. This same principle applies across every search screen in JobDiva, not just here at the top. Notice too the small microphone icon at the right edge of the search bar — you can search by voice instead of typing if your hands are busy — and the sparkle icon beside it, which signals JobDiva's AI-assisted search suggestions kicking in as you type. It's worth exploring both icons once, just to see what each returns.

Next to search sits Favorites — you can star up to nine apps here as quick shortcuts. These are admin-preset for your specific role, and while you can technically toggle them yourself through Hide or Show Apps, we strongly recommend leaving them alone, since they're already calibrated to exactly what you need day to day. This is that Hide or Show Apps screen — you can star any app here, or reset to the default layout entirely if you want to start over.

The Alerts icon shows your own JobDiva activity — status changes, new assignments, job description edits, all logged right here with a timestamp. Many of these alerts are triggered behind the scenes by VMS synchronization, sometimes called the Codler — an integration that automatically feeds job requirements from a client's Vendor Management System directly into JobDiva, so new positions and updates can appear without anyone manually re-entering them. Scanning this list regularly is a quick way to stay on top of what's actually changed since you last logged in. It's a small habit that pays off quickly.

1.3.text: The News icon keeps you current on JobDiva enhancements and updates. Take a look at this notification feed — every entry here represents something new: system changes, scheduled maintenance, and feature rollouts. Click into one, like this Automated AI Posting Descriptions enhancement, and you'll see the full write-up of what it does and how to turn it on. That's a good example of the AI-assisted features JobDiva has been rolling out, like automated job description editing. Keep in mind that exactly which features are active for you depends on how your company has customized the platform, so don't worry if what you see here doesn't match everything in your own account. Notice the Search box in the corner of this list, along with the Category column you can sort by — handy when you're hunting for one specific update rather than scrolling the whole feed. You can also control how many entries display at once using the dropdown up top. It's a small detail, but it saves real time.

As you keep scrolling this same list, you'll notice the entries aren't only enhancements — there are Update entries too, like this change to License and Certification alert logic, and dedicated Training entries pointing you toward upcoming webinars, which is exactly what we'll walk through next. Down at the bottom of the table you can also page through older notifications, so nothing ever really disappears from this history — if you want to check exactly when a feature rolled out, or reread an announcement from a few months back, it's all still here, sorted by date published. Getting into the habit of skimming this list once a week, even for thirty seconds, is enough to catch a policy change or a new AI feature before a client or a colleague asks you about it and catches you off guard. If you ever need to find something specific rather than browse chronologically, that same Search box works here too — just start typing a keyword from the title. If a webinar you want conflicts with your schedule, don't worry — most of these get recorded and stay listed here afterward, so you can catch up on your own time instead of having to attend live.

Under News, you'll also find a dedicated Training tab, and it's worth spending a minute here. Scrolling through the schedule, you'll see role-specific webinars for just about every part of the business: Onboarding 101 and 102 for getting comfortable with the basics, Team Leader and Administration Training for anyone stepping into management, Intro to JobDiva and Recruiter Training for people brand new to recruiting in the system, Intro to CRM for client-relationship and business-development teams, and Advanced BI for reporting once you've outgrown the fundamentals. There's also a session dedicated to AI features, covering tools like Global Prompts and AI-generated resume summaries. And importantly, keep an eye out for the dedicated Healthcare Recruiting webinar. If you're working in healthcare staffing, that one is genuinely worth your time — it covers the Job page, profession-and-specialty searching, and other workflows you simply won't find in the general training. New sessions get added regularly, so it's worth checking back. It's a packed schedule, worth revisiting. Notice each entry lists an exact date and time in Eastern Time, along with a direct Register Now link you can click right from this same popup — no need to hunt for a separate sign-up page.

Each listing also tells you who the session is meant for — notice how Recruiter Training and Intro to CRM both recommend attending Intro to JobDiva first, so JobDiva is actually suggesting a rough order to take these in if you're brand new. If a live time doesn't work with your schedule, don't skip it entirely — check with your manager, since many of these webinars get recorded and shared afterward for anyone who couldn't attend live. And don't just register for the ones aimed at total beginners: even a session like Advanced BI or the dedicated AI-Powered Features webinar, covering things like Global Prompts and AI-generated resume summaries, is worth bookmarking for later, once you're past the fundamentals and ready to go deeper. Take thirty seconds now to scan which sessions apply to your specific role, and register for those today, and keep an eye out for new sessions, since JobDiva adds them here regularly. One more practical note: these sessions repeat on a rotation, so if this week's schedule doesn't line up with yours, the same webinar will almost certainly show up again within a month or two. And if you ever lose track of which ones you've registered for, your calendar invite from JobDiva will still be sitting in your inbox as a reminder, so there's no need to keep a separate list. Bookmark this Help library in your own head, not just in your browser — knowing it exists is honestly the harder part; once you remember to check here first, finding the actual article is easy.

For quick, in-the-moment answers, use the Help icon. It opens this Help and Best Practices library, organized by topic — categories like AI Features, Candidate and Resume Features, CRM, and Email — so you can browse straight to an article, the way we just did here. But even faster: click the chat icon in the top right to open Ask Diva, JobDiva's built-in chatbot. Type your question, and you'll get an immediate answer. Get in the habit of checking the Help icon and the chatbot before escalating a question to JobDiva support — most day-to-day questions about a specific feature can be resolved right there without ever opening a support ticket, and it's simply faster for everyone involved. Notice how Ask Diva greets you by name — 'What can I help you with today, Steve?' — and responds right in this side panel without you ever leaving the page you're on. That's the fastest way to get unstuck: a quick question typed here almost always beats digging through a help article or waiting on a support reply. Both are there so you're never stuck waiting on someone else's schedule.

1.4.text: Your profile icon lets you sign out, verify your details, and confirm your division is set correctly — and if it's wrong, request a correction from your admin team rather than trying to work around it yourself, since the wrong division can affect what you're able to see and do elsewhere in the system. One essential, easy-to-overlook detail: accessing JobDiva outside office hours or off the office network requires a VPN, which is set up through your IT team, not something you can configure on your own. Scrolling further down your profile, you'll find additional sections for assigning permissions, setting your default tab, and configuring calendar, email, text, and browser tool options — plus your time zone and region, which matters if you or your team span multiple offices. There's also a personal link here you can send directly to candidates so they can self-register on the portal, saving you the step of entering their information manually. None of this requires admin help; it's yours to adjust, so it's worth taking a few minutes early on to set your defaults exactly the way you want them. Take five minutes the first week to actually open each of these settings once, so nothing here feels unfamiliar later.

Finally, let's look at the left navigation. The Homepage icon, right here, always returns you to your role-based homepage, no matter how deep you've navigated into the system. Hover over it for a second, as we're doing now, and you'll see a small tooltip simply confirming 'Home' — a nice way to double check you're clicking the right icon before you commit, especially early on when all these icons still look unfamiliar. It's a small habit that saves you from accidentally landing somewhere you didn't intend. The same trick works for every icon on this rail.

The interface itself is organized into what are called Bars — grouped sections like Sourcing and Jobs, which you can see expand right here — and each Bar contains individual Applications, like Talent Search, which are the specific clickable tools you'll actually use every day. Understanding this Bars-and-Applications structure now will make everything in the rest of this course click into place much faster.

2.1.text: Your User Dashboard is a personal, fully customizable home base — and it's yours to shape around how you actually work. Right here you can see widgets like your sales activity for the week, current employees, contact and candidate notes, onboarding status, call metrics, and even a weekly to-do list. Each of these widgets ties to real goals, too — notice the progress bars under My Sales Activity for the Week, tracking your actual external submittals, interviews, and starts against the specific goal your manager has set for each. If you click Customize now, exactly like this, you'll see the full list of available panels open in a scrollable window — everything from External Links your team leaders have added, to My Actions for the Week, to Submittal Due Dates below it. Spend a few minutes exploring this panel list, even if you don't add anything yet.

Click Customize, and you'll see you can add or remove widgets to fit how you work — options like My Actions for the Week, Submittal Due Dates, My Recruiting Activities, and something called your Active Opportunities Funnel, which gives you a visual sense of where your open deals stand across each stage. Once you've picked what you want, click Apply Changes, and the dashboard reloads with your new layout in place — you can always come back and adjust it later. Notice too that hovering over any point on these charts pops up the exact figure for that week, instead of leaving you to guess from the line alone. Either way, nothing you pick here is permanent or risky to experiment with.

Here's the most important thing to understand about your dashboard: it's only as accurate as your data entry. Notice this funnel here — it's showing no opportunities to display, simply because the activity behind it hasn't been logged. If jobs and candidate actions aren't recorded in real time — submissions, interviews, status changes — your dashboard won't reflect reality, no matter how well you've customized it. That's a discipline issue on the recruiter's side, not a limitation of JobDiva itself. Just below the dashboard on the left rail sits the clock-shaped History icon — hovering over it, as we're doing now, brings up a simple tooltip labeled History, and clicking it takes you to a completely different kind of log, one built from your own clicks rather than your data entry. We'll walk through exactly what that log looks like and how to use it in just a moment.

The History section complements your dashboard by giving you a click-history log of every candidate, job, and page you've opened, organized by day and filterable by date. So if you ever need to retrace your steps from earlier in the day or week, you can always find your way back here without having to remember exact names or job numbers. Notice this log is split into three columns — Candidates, Jobs, and Pages — each with its own dropdown arrow so you can collapse a section you don't need right now. Entries are grouped by day: Today, Yesterday, and Earlier Than Yesterday, with a timestamp next to each one. So if you clicked into a candidate like this one yesterday afternoon, or opened a specific job order, or even just visited a page like Edit My Profile or the Help Section, it's all sitting right here, in the order you actually did it. This is especially useful after a long day juggling a dozen open tabs, when you're trying to remember which candidate record you were looking at an hour ago, or which job you meant to follow up on before you got pulled into something else. It's a simple tool, but experienced recruiters lean on it constantly, precisely because it never requires you to remember anything on your own.

2.2.text: Before we go further, one important rule: never edit Settings yourself. Any change you need goes through your manager, who escalates it to the admin team or the SuperAdmin — this keeps the system consistent for everyone. Now let's look at the big picture, right here in your Applications menu: JobDiva is organized around four functional bars. You'll see them laid out right here in this same menu — Sourcing, Jobs, Analytics, and Engagement, each with its own colored bar.

Sourcing handles candidate management and allocation — this is where you'll spend a huge amount of your time. Jobs, right alongside it, handles job management and allocation, working hand-in-hand with Sourcing. Notice the icons underneath: My Jobs and My Jobs as Primary separate the roles you're secondary versus primary on, Search Jobs and New Job cover finding and creating job orders, and the two dashboard icons give you a quick visual snapshot of everything you're tracking. Being the 'Primary' recruiter on a job usually just means you're the one who gets credited if it's filled, which matters for tracking and, frankly, for commission. Keep that distinction in mind as you start getting assigned to jobs.

Analytics covers reporting and ratings, but access here is individually restricted by role, so don't be surprised if you can't see everything a manager can. And Engagement covers your calendar, tasks, and interviews — it's used somewhat differently between IT and healthcare recruiting, which we'll get into later in the course. As a recruiter, you'll spend most of your time living in Sourcing and Jobs, with Analytics and parts of Engagement being more manager-facing tools that you'll use occasionally rather than constantly. Notice too you can hover over any of these icons, like Reports here under Analytics, to get a quick preview before you commit to clicking in. It's a habit worth building early.

3.1.text: Let's open the Jobs bar. My Jobs shows every open job that's currently assigned to you — the full list you're responsible for, at a glance. Notice everything laid out right here in the table: issue date, job title, client company, hiring manager, location, current status, priority, bill rate, start date, and submittal due date, so you can size up your entire workload without opening a single job record.

My Jobs as Primary narrows that same list down to jobs where you're specifically the Primary Recruiter — meaning you carry lead responsibility for filling them, as opposed to a Secondary Recruiter, who's assigned to assist but doesn't own the outcome. Here in the Job Status filter, you can toggle between views like My Open Jobs, My Primary Open Jobs, and All My Primary Jobs to see exactly which positions fall into each bucket. And notice the Users column on the right: those tags — PR, S, and PS — mark out Primary Recruiter, Secondary Recruiter, and Primary Sales on every job. Primary Sales refers to the account manager you actually submit candidates to once you've found a match.

Beyond the Job Status filter, notice you can also narrow this list by Issued Date. Click into either date box, and a calendar picker like this one drops down, so you can set a from-date and a to-date without typing anything by hand. Set a range — say, the first few weeks of August — and click Display, and the list refreshes immediately. Watch what happens: our five open jobs narrow down to just one, because only that job was issued inside the window we picked. That's a genuinely useful habit whenever you want to see what's landed recently versus what's been sitting open for a while. While we're looking at this table, it's worth calling out a few more columns you'll use constantly. The Harvest column shows sourcing status — 'On Schedule' here means recruiting activity for that job is tracking against plan. Priority flags urgency, like the High Priority tag on that first correctional RN role, telling you exactly where to focus first when your day gets busy. Max Bill Rate gives you the ceiling you can quote a client for that position, which matters the moment you start negotiating a candidate's pay rate against the spread. And don't overlook Start Date versus Submittal Due Date — those are two different deadlines: one is when the client wants the person working, the other is when the client wants your submissions in hand, and mixing the two up is a common mistake for new recruiters. You can also click any column header — Issued, Title, Status, whatever you need — to re-sort the whole list on the fly. And take a look at the Ref# and JobDiva# columns sitting right here in the table: both numbers are visible without opening the job at all, so for a quick lookup you often don't even need to leave this screen. One more habit worth building here: get comfortable re-sorting by more than one column before you commit to a plan for the day — sort by Priority first to see what's urgent, then by Submittal Due Date to see what's actually running out of time, since those two aren't always the same job. A High Priority tag doesn't automatically mean the clock is tightest; sometimes a lower-priority job simply has a nearer deadline, and this table is exactly where you'd catch that before it becomes a problem. Give yourself a moment to just sit with this table before you start filtering anything — knowing what every column means up front makes every filter you apply afterward far more deliberate.

Once you're done drilling into a specific date range, remember to clear those Issued Date fields and hit Display again — that resets you back to the full list of five jobs, so you don't accidentally keep working from a filtered view and think a job has disappeared when it's really just been filtered out. Now watch the Job Status dropdown itself. Switching it from My Open Jobs Only to My Primary Open Jobs and clicking Display immediately drops our count from five jobs down to three — those are the positions where this recruiter is specifically the Primary Recruiter rather than just a Secondary. That's the exact distinction we walked through a moment ago, now showing up as real, different numbers on screen, which is a good way to sanity-check that you understand your own workload correctly. It's worth building a habit of checking this Primary-only view regularly, separate from your full list. Since you carry lead responsibility on these jobs, they're the ones where your activity — submissions, interviews, fill rate — actually gets tracked against you in performance reporting. A Secondary Recruiter role is meant to be supportive; you might source candidates or help with scheduling, but the outcome isn't scored against your name the same way. So if you only have time to work a handful of jobs today, this filtered list tells you exactly which ones matter most to your own numbers. It's a small motion — clear the fields, hit Display, done — but skipping it is a surprisingly common way new recruiters convince themselves a job vanished when it's simply hidden by a filter they forgot was still active. Build the habit of glancing at that Issued Date box every time you open this screen fresh, before you even start scanning the list, so you know exactly what you're looking at.

Let's back out to the Apps menu now and look at where Search Jobs sits alongside everything else in the Jobs section. You've got My Jobs and My Jobs as Primary, which we just spent time in; New Job, which is where you'll go to manually create a job record from scratch whenever a requirement doesn't sync in automatically — that's exactly what the next lesson covers in detail; and then My Jobs Dashboard and My Primary Jobs Dashboard, which give you a more visual, metrics-driven view of these same assigned jobs — issue date, division, title, location, bill and salary rate, status, priority, and submission activity — all summarized so you can scan your entire workload without opening a single record. We'll spend real time inside those dashboards later in this course. For now, though, click into Search Jobs, since that's the tool you'll reach for anytime you need to track down one specific position rather than browse everything currently assigned to you. Notice right away that this page looks different from the simple table we were just using — it's a much more detailed search form, with sections for Duration, Location, Pay, Qualifications, and User-Defined Fields all the way down the page. You'll also see filters for Sector, Professions, and Specialties, plus a full Location panel over on the right for city, state, zip, and country — useful when you're casting a wide net across an entire region. That's because Search Jobs is built to search across every job in the entire system, not just the ones assigned to you, so it needs far more filters to narrow things down. Don't let the number of fields intimidate you, though — in practice you'll only ever need one or two of them to find exactly what you're looking for, and that's what we're about to look at. We'll leave most of that untouched today. Let's dive in. Take a slow first pass down the page without touching anything, just to get oriented — notice how Duration, Location, and Pay each get their own dedicated section rather than being crammed into one form, which is exactly why the page feels so much longer than My Jobs. Once you've searched by ID or Reference Number a few times, though, you'll find yourself scrolling straight past nearly all of it, since those two fields alone answer most of what you actually need day to day.

When you need to search for a job rather than browse your assigned list, this Search Jobs screen is the fastest way in. Right here you'll find fields for the JobDiva Reference Number and an Optional Reference Number — use either one, and the system pulls up the exact job in seconds. Remember the distinction: the JobDiva ID is generated automatically by the system the moment a job is created, while the Reference ID is the number assigned by the client itself. Searching by either of these IDs is dramatically faster and more reliable than typing in a job title, which can match dozens of similar postings across different clients. Let's try it now. Typing the JobDiva Reference Number — 26-04635, in this case — straight into that field and clicking Search takes us directly to that one exact job, no scrolling, no guessing which of several similarly titled postings is the right one. That's the whole point: a job title like 'Interviewer' or 'Registered Nurse' might match dozens of open requisitions across different clients, but a JobDiva ID or client Reference ID is unique to that single job, every time. Make it a habit to grab whichever ID you have — from an email, a client portal, or a teammate's message — and search by that first, before you ever try a title or company name. That single habit alone will save you real time every single day. Once you're comfortable with that shortcut, head back to the Apps menu and you're ready to move into creating jobs yourself, which is exactly where we're going next.

3.2.text: Now let's create a job from scratch. You'll do this manually whenever automatic sync from a client's Vendor Management System fails, or when a requirement arrives by email instead of through the system. When that happens, this New Job screen is where you'll build the record field by field. Basic Info up top captures the Title, Position Type, and an Optional Reference Number — that's the client's own job number, separate from the JobDiva ID the system will generate once you save. Just below that you'll set the job's Status, which starts as OPEN, and its Priority, so anyone glancing at your job list later knows how urgently it needs to be filled. Notice the Healthcare Sector field sitting right next to Priority — that's specific to healthcare postings, and you'll set it to something like Service or Clinical depending on the role. Then come Contact, Company, Division, and the full address block — city, state, country, zip — followed further down by Scheduling, Billing, and Compensation sections. We'll walk through each of these in order, but the key habit to build right now is this: fill in every field you have information for, even the ones that feel optional, because incomplete job records cause real confusion for everyone downstream. Take it section by section rather than trying to fill everything in at once — rushing through a form this long is exactly how a required field ends up skipped by accident, and an incomplete job record downstream is always harder to untangle than the few extra seconds spent here.

Accurately completing every structured field on this form — title, specialty, position type, division, client, facility, complete address, schedule, and billing details — is what we call JobDiva Cleaning, and it matters because every downstream step depends on this data being correct. Two details deserve special attention here. First, always select the Division that matches your own vertical, IT or healthcare, since the available options genuinely differ between the two, and picking the wrong one can misroute the job entirely.

Let's actually see that Division difference in action. Watch what happens when I switch this dropdown from Healthcare to Information Technology — the whole form reshapes itself. The Healthcare Sector field disappears, along with the separate Overtime and Doubletime rate rows, and in their place you get IT-specific fields: a Bill Rate and Pay Rate range instead of a flat number, Start and End dates, a Submittal Due date, Openings, Max Allowed Submittals, an Experience Level dropdown, and an Onsite, Remote, or Hybrid setting. Switch it back to Healthcare and all of those Healthcare-specific fields — Sector, the itemized Overtime and Doubletime rate rows — return. This is exactly why picking the right Division before you fill anything else in really matters: get it wrong, and you'll end up entering data into fields that don't even apply to this job. Get in the habit of setting Division first, before touching anything else on this form, so every field you fill in afterward is actually the right one for this job's vertical.

Next, in Company slash Department, start typing a client's name — type just 'aya' and JobDiva's autocomplete immediately suggests Aya Healthcare, so you're not stuck typing out full company names from memory. Once you select the company, a Facility field appears underneath it, and choosing a specific facility — like this Abbott Northwestern Hospital location — automatically fills in the entire address block for you: street, city, state, and zip, all populated instantly. That's a real time-saver, and it also protects you from typos in an address that a client, or a candidate reading the job description later, might notice. Down in Billing, you can also click that plus icon to add extra pay-rate rows beyond the standard rate — Holiday pay is a common one to add for healthcare shifts that span holidays, each with its own rate you set independently. Up in Scheduling, set a Start date, and if known, an End date and Duration — there's also a Job Schedule link for entering more detailed shift patterns when hours aren't a simple standard week. That autofilled address is worth a quick glance before you move on, too — facility records occasionally lag behind a real-world move or renovation, and catching a stale address here is far easier than a candidate flagging it after they've already shown up for a shift.

Once you've set the job's schedule, move down to Billing. And even though JobDiva doesn't currently use the bill rate to auto-calculate total compensation, enter it anyway — that data still matters for reporting and for anyone reviewing the job later.

Clicking that Job Schedule link opens a more detailed scheduling window, where you set exact shift start and end times, pick specific working days, and even flag non-working days eligible for stipends — all rolling up into a total hours-per-week calculation. Below that, both Billing and Compensation let you stack on extra pay-rate rows beyond the standard rate, for things like Holiday pay, plus separate sections for Orientation hours, Stipends, and total weekly compensation, so every piece of what a candidate will actually be paid lives in one place.

Second, never skip the Submitted Due Date field — it's mandatory, not optional, and job records without it create real confusion downstream for anyone tracking deadlines. Notice it's already filled in right here — 08/27/2026 — alongside Openings and Experience Level. Scroll down from here and you'll land on the Requirements tab, which is exactly where we're headed next.

3.3.text: With the core fields complete, it's time for Job Description Cleaning — and note this is a genuinely separate process from JobDiva Cleaning, focused purely on formatting the description text itself, since that text syncs live to external job boards and your company website the moment you save. Let's open a blank document and build a quick checklist before we touch any formatting, so nothing important gets lost once we start writing.

A strong job description follows three parts: an introduction to the role, the required qualifications or must-haves, and any preferred or desired skills that are nice-to-have but not deal-breakers. Before you write any of that narrative, though, it helps to lay out the basics first — position, location, duration, shift timing and type, and any visa requirements — so nothing gets missed once you start drafting.

Let's actually build that basics checklist together, since seeing it done once makes it much easier to repeat on your own. Start a quick document — even a plain text file works — and jot down Position or Title or Role: in this case, RN. Then Location: the full address of the facility, not just a city name, since candidates want to know exactly where they'd be working. Then Duration: say, twelve weeks for a typical travel contract. And then Shift Timing and Shift Type: days, nights, or rotating, plus whether it's an eight, ten, or twelve-hour shift. If the role has any visa sponsorship requirements or restrictions, jot that down here too, before you ever start writing the narrative sections. Having all of this laid out in five or six short lines means that when you sit down to actually write the introduction and the qualifications, you're filling in prose around facts you've already nailed down, instead of hunting for them mid-sentence. This is a small habit, but it saves real time, especially on busy days when you're cleaning several job descriptions back to back and don't want to lose track of which detail belongs to which posting. Keep the checklist open in a second window as you draft, so you're always cross-referencing rather than relying on memory. Notice this checklist isn't meant to be elegant — it's meant to be fast and complete. Even a messy list of six short lines beats a polished paragraph that's missing the one detail a candidate actually needed, like shift length or contract duration, so don't overthink the format here.

For the introduction, describe the role and what the organization is looking for — you can even draft it with an AI assistant to get started faster, then edit it to fit. From there, list your required qualifications: the licenses, certifications, and core responsibilities a candidate absolutely must have to be considered.

Let's put that into practice. Pasting a quick AI-generated draft for the introduction gives us a solid starting paragraph — it names the role, the setting, and the core purpose of the position in just a few sentences. That's a perfectly good first pass, but don't just paste and save it as-is. Read it over, swap in the specifics from your basics checklist — the actual facility, shift pattern, and duration — and trim anything that sounds generic or repeats itself. Treat an AI draft as raw material you shape, never as a finished product you publish untouched. Give that draft one more read before moving on, specifically checking that it doesn't quietly repeat a qualification you're about to list separately in the Required section below — overlap between the intro and the bullets is one of the easiest things to miss on a fast first pass.

From there, build out the Required Qualifications section as a bulleted list rather than a paragraph — it's far easier for a candidate to scan. For this RN role, that list covers the core clinical responsibilities: assessing, monitoring, and documenting patient health status; administering medications, treatments, and IV therapies as prescribed; developing individualized nursing care plans; collaborating with physicians and the broader care team; educating patients and families; maintaining accurate records; responding promptly to emergencies; and staying compliant with infection control and safety standards. Underneath that, list the actual qualifications a candidate must hold to even be considered — starting with an active Registered Nurse license, and going on to any required certifications, years of experience, or specialty training. Every one of these bullets should describe something that's genuinely non-negotiable; save the nice-to-haves for the next section.

Once the Required section is solid, save the document and take a breath before moving to Preferred. It's worth pausing here to talk about that Shift Timing line from our basics checklist, because it behaves differently depending on which side of the business you're on. On the IT side, shift timing is usually fixed and straightforward — a standard nine-to-five, or a set remote schedule agreed to upfront, and it rarely changes once the job is posted. On the healthcare side, shift timing varies constantly: days, nights, evenings, rotating schedules, weekend differentials, even shift length itself can shift between eight, ten, and twelve hours depending on the unit and the facility. That's exactly why we captured Shift Timing as its own line on the checklist, separate from Shift Type — in healthcare, get that detail wrong in the posting, and you'll field confused questions from candidates before you've even had a chance to screen them. Keep that distinction in mind as we finish out this job description. Before you copy any of this over into JobDiva's actual Job Description field, scroll back up and check every line in your basics checklist against what you've written — position, location, duration, both shift lines, and any notes — to make sure nothing got left out along the way. It's a two-minute check that catches most mistakes before a candidate ever sees them. Once that's confirmed, you're ready to move into the Preferred section, which is what we'll build out next. That habit alone will save you from the single most common JD complaint clients raise: missing or wrong basic facts. It's worth doing this same cross-check on every job description you write, not just this one, since it's the fastest way to catch a mismatched fact before a candidate does — and candidates notice mismatched facts far more often than recruiters expect, especially around shift timing and duration. Building that habit now, on this very first job description, is what makes it automatic by the tenth one.

Then round it out with your preferred or desired skills — the nice-to-haves that make a candidate stand out but aren't deal-breakers if missing. Keep the formatting simple throughout: minimal paragraph spacing, sparing use of highlights, and underline reserved only for section titles — a clean, scannable description reads far better to candidates than a dense wall of text. And here's a firm rule worth repeating: never include a client's sensitive or contract information in a public posting. If you want to share the client's actual name with a candidate, do that manually by email — don't put it in the posted description where anyone can see it.

Notice the trainer circles back here to fill in that Shift Timing line on the checklist we started with, now that the rest of the posting has clarified it — that's completely normal; you don't have to nail every field in order on the first pass. Also notice a 'Key Responsibilities' heading gets added right above that bulleted list of duties, separating it clearly from the Qualifications section underneath — small structural touches like that make a long description dramatically easier for a candidate to skim on their phone. Small touches like that heading are easy to skip when you're moving quickly, but they cost seconds to add and noticeably change how skimmable the finished posting feels to a candidate reading it on a phone.

Now here's the formatting rule in action. Open the Paragraph dialog and check the Spacing settings — Before and After should both be at zero, or as close to it as your template allows, and go ahead and check 'Don't add space between paragraphs of the same style.' Watch what happens to the page count once that's applied: this same document, all two pages of it, collapses down to a single page instantly, just by tightening the spacing. That's the entire point of minimal paragraph spacing — it's not about looking sparse, it's about fitting more real information in front of a candidate's eyes before they lose interest and stop scrolling. That single formatting change is worth remembering for every job description you touch going forward — it costs you ten seconds and nothing else, and it's the difference between a posting that reads as tight and professional and one that reads as an unedited wall of text.

One more Preferred bullet gets added here — Compact License, which for a traveling RN role means the nursing license is valid across multiple states under the interstate compact, a genuinely useful thing to flag as a preference rather than a requirement. Once the whole description reads clean, copy it in full and paste it straight into the Job Description field back in JobDiva — that's the field that syncs live out to your job boards and company website, so this is the version the outside world actually sees. Scroll down past it and you'll notice the Requirements section is already waiting below, prefilled with a Registered Nurse license requirement for both external submittals and starts, along with a Users section showing who's assigned and empty Remarks and Notes fields. That's exactly where this lesson picks up next — the Requirements tab and User assignment, which is how you'll finish setting up this job before saving it for good. Take one more pass over the whole document before you paste it anywhere — read it out loud if you can, since anything that sounds awkward spoken usually reads awkward too. Check that every bullet uses parallel phrasing, that you haven't repeated the same qualification in both the Required and Preferred sections, and that nothing about the client's identity or contract terms slipped into the text by accident. A five-minute proofread here saves you from an embarrassing correction email to a client later, and it's the last real checkpoint before this job description goes live for candidates to see.

3.4.text: Two tabs remain before saving. The Requirements tab captures a client's compliance needs — things like vaccination status, shift preferences, and other qualifications specific to that particular position — and this becomes especially important in healthcare, where it ties directly into what's called the Submittal Packet.

Let's open that Requirements tab and see it in action. Right at the top, License Requirements shows our Registered Nurse license, with checkboxes for External Submittal, Start, and Non-Expired Document — check External Submittal and Start here, and JobDiva will enforce that any candidate submitted, or any candidate who actually starts the assignment, has to have that license on file. Below that, General Requirements gives you a checklist of common compliance items — W2, Travel, Security Clearance, References, OT, Drug Test, and Background Check — each with its own External Submittal and Start checkboxes, so you can flag exactly when in the process each one needs to be satisfied. In our example here, we've checked Security Clearance and References as required before submittal, and Drug Test and Background Check as required before the candidate actually starts — which makes sense, since a client usually wants to see references before they'll even consider someone, but a drug screen typically happens closer to the start date. One more thing: click Add Qualification to create a custom requirement — here we've added 'Shift Preference is Day' as its own item, checked for both External Submittal and Start, since this client treats day-shift-only as a hard requirement, not just a note. Take the same care here that you did with the core job fields — a Requirements tab that's only half filled in creates exactly the kind of downstream confusion this whole cleaning process is meant to prevent.
The User tab is where a manager, and only a manager, assigns Primary and Secondary Recruiters along with Primary and Secondary Sales roles for the job. You as a recruiter can't self-assign here.

Here's what that actually looks like on screen: the Users modal gives a manager a searchable list of every user in the system on the left, plus saved Group Lists to speed up repetitive assignments, and a Manage Roles table on the right with checkboxes for Sales, Primary Sales, Recruiter, Primary Recruiter, Secondary Recruiter, and Secondary Sales for each person added. Check the right boxes, hit Save, and a quick summary confirms exactly who's now the Recruiter and who's the Primary Recruiter on this job. That kind of role visibility is exactly why this assignment step matters beyond just paperwork — anyone on the team who opens this job afterward can see at a glance who owns it, without having to ask around.

The good news is you'll always know the moment you've been assigned, because JobDiva sends you an automatic email notification the instant it happens — no need to keep checking back. Once the Requirements and User tabs are in order, add any extra client context in the Remarks field.

Before you save, scroll back up and give the whole form one more look, top to bottom — Basic Info, Requirements, and the User tab you just set — since a mistake caught now takes ten seconds to fix, but the same mistake caught after a candidate's already been submitted can mean starting over.

Then click Save. That single action finalizes the job record and generates its unique JobDiva ID, which you'll use from that point forward to reference this exact position. Once it saves, this View/Edit Job screen appears, JobDiva ID at the top, with tabs for Requirements, Candidates, and Activity below.

3.5.text: Now that we've created a job and saved it, let's shift from building job records to actually monitoring them. Once a job's live, you don't want to keep clicking into individual records just to check status — that's what dashboards are for. Head back to the Apps menu, and in the Jobs section you'll see two dashboard tiles sitting right next to the ones we've already used: My Jobs Dashboard and My Primary Jobs Dashboard. Click into My Jobs Dashboard first, since it covers every job assigned to you, not just the ones where you're Primary. Before we dive in, here's a quick recap of what just happened in the last lesson: we built a brand-new RN job for Aya Healthcare from scratch, cleaned up its Job Description, set its compliance Requirements, and assigned ourselves as the Recruiter. That job now has its own JobDiva ID and is sitting live in the system, exactly like every other job on your list. The dashboards we're about to open don't just apply to jobs like that one you build yourself — they roll up every job you touch, whether it came in through automatic sync, an email requirement, or manual entry, into one place you can scan in seconds. Take a moment to appreciate how much groundwork that represents — a cleaned job description, compliance requirements locked in, the right recruiter assigned — before a single candidate has even been sourced. That's where this dashboard starts paying off, so let's open it now and walk through exactly what it tracks for you. Notice, too, that none of this dashboard work requires you to remember which jobs you touched recently or dig back through old emails — it's all already sitting here, organized and current, the moment you open the page. That's really the whole value proposition of a dashboard like this: it turns 'let me go check on that' into a five-second glance. Give yourself a second to actually look at the tile layout here before clicking in — knowing both dashboards exist side by side is half the value, since you'll be choosing between them constantly once you're juggling more than a handful of open jobs.

My Job Dashboard gives you a working view of every job assigned to you — issue date, division, title, location, client, bill and salary rate, status, priority, and submission activity, all laid out in one table so you can scan your entire workload at a glance.

Scroll across and you'll see this exact table broken into four automatically-grouped sections: jobs with no submittals yet, submittals pending interviews, jobs already covered for submittals, and jobs that are fully filled — each labeled right in the page so you don't have to hunt for them. Keep scrolling right, past Bill Rate and Salary, and you'll find columns for submissions, rejections, interviews, and hires — the entire funnel for every job, laid out side by side.

Two filters here are especially useful day to day. 'Open jobs with no submitters' flags positions assigned to you where you haven't submitted a single candidate yet — a clear signal about where to focus next. And 'pending interviews' flags jobs where an interview actually happened but its status was never updated in JobDiva, which is a paperwork gap, not a real scheduling problem.

Scroll further right on this same dashboard and you'll find the real payoff columns: Internal and External Submittals, Internal and External Rejects, Interviews, Hires, and Pending counts. Look at that Filled Open Jobs row at the bottom — twenty-nine internal submittals, four internal rejects, thirty external submittals, two external rejects, twenty-two interviews, and sixteen hires, all for a single Interviewer position in Martinsville. That's the entire lifecycle of a job, from first submission to final hire, visible in one row without opening a single candidate record.

Head back to the Apps menu now, right next to My Jobs Dashboard, and you'll spot My Primary Jobs Dashboard — same exact layout, same columns, but filtered down to only the jobs where you're the Primary Recruiter, mirroring the same Primary-versus-Secondary distinction we covered back when we looked at My Jobs versus My Jobs as Primary. If you only have time to check one dashboard on a busy day, this Primary-filtered view is usually the better use of those few minutes, since it's your name that gets tied to the numbers in performance reporting. Click into it now, and give it a second to load — you'll see the same four sections rebuild themselves: Open Jobs with No Submittals, Submittals Pending Interviews, Covered Open Jobs, and Filled Open Jobs, just recalculated against your Primary-only workload instead of everything you touch. For a recruiter juggling a dozen or more open positions at once, that narrower slice is often the difference between a five-minute morning check-in and getting lost scrolling through jobs that aren't really yours to drive. Keep that habit going forward: a quick pass through this view, first thing each day, tells you exactly where your attention is needed most. And if a number here ever looks off — a hire that isn't showing, an interview that seems to be missing — the first place to look is always the underlying job record itself, since this dashboard can only ever be as current as the statuses recruiters have actually saved there.

At the individual job level, there's also a cumulative dashboard that totals one position's submissions, interviews, and hires over its entire lifetime. Both views share the same dependency: their accuracy relies entirely on recruiters updating statuses in real time, in what's called the node section — something we'll cover in detail later in this course. Get in the habit of checking these dashboards regularly, and always keep your own job statuses current — the whole system is only as accurate as the updates you actually make.

4.1.text: Analytics houses JobDiva's reporting tools, and it's worth knowing upfront that most of what lives here is manager-facing rather than something you'll use constantly as a recruiter. The Submittal Matrix Report checks submittals by user, department, or date range, and it's primarily a manager's tool for tracking recruiter output — submissions, interviews, and hires — across a team or time period. On screen, filters let you narrow results by job type, priority, division, or company type, and choose specific users or an entire group to report on. Running the report produces a breakdown table showing jobs assigned, submittals, interviews, and hires for each user, exportable straight to Excel.

A related activity and summary report breaks the same kind of data down by client, group, or division instead of by individual user, which is useful for spotting patterns across an entire book of business. On the filter screen, you can narrow results by job type, priority, job division, or company type, and select specific users to include. Once your filters are set, you choose an output format — HTML, CSV, or PDF — and generate either a visual report with charts, or a regular report with the plain tabular breakdown, and you can even schedule it to run automatically.

One thing to keep in mind: recruiter access to these reports is individually authorized, meaning your manager or admin controls exactly which reports you personally can open. So if a colleague can pull a report you can't see, that's not a bug — it simply reflects how access has been configured for your specific role, and if you genuinely need it for your work, that's a conversation to have with your manager.

4.2.text: The Engagement bar starts with My Calendar, where you can schedule events directly tied to your recruiting work — set a subject, link a specific candidate, choose a time and recurrence type, add a location and description, and save; JobDiva automatically emails the invite to everyone involved the moment you do. You'll also choose an event type from a dropdown — Appointment, Reminder, Demo, or one of several presentation categories — and you can add attendees by searching the Users or Groups tabs and dragging names into the Attendees column. Once saved, the event drops right onto your calendar grid for that day and time, color-coded so it's easy to spot at a glance.

One thing worth flagging: Outlook sync for the calendar was noted as temporarily non-functional at the time this training was recorded, due to a known technical issue, so it's worth verifying the current status locally before relying on it for anything time-sensitive. With that noted, let's shift over to Tasks, which live in this same Engagement area right next to the calendar and cover action items rather than scheduled meetings.

Tasks work in a similar spirit to calendar events but for action items rather than meetings: you can assign a task to a colleague, a recruiter, a manager, or even a candidate, with a due date, a task type, and a completion percentage to track progress. Picking the due date opens a small calendar picker, and the Task Type dropdown offers a long list of presets — things like Contact Second Follow-Up Call or a general Contact Reminder — so you're rarely typing one from scratch. The completion percentage lets you nudge progress up as you work through the task.

Saving a task sends an immediate notification email to whoever it's assigned to, exactly like calendar events do — which is exactly why it's worth double-checking every detail before you hit save, since there's no quiet way to walk it back. One practical habit worth building: check both your calendar and your task list first thing each morning, since this is often where your day's real priorities live. If a task turns out unnecessary after saving, you can still edit or delete it — the email just won't undo itself, so a quick follow-up message is the polite fix.

4.3.text: JobDiva includes two distinct interview tools, and it's worth understanding when each one fits. Live Interviews let you video-interview a candidate directly inside the platform — you can share an instant link for right now, or schedule a specific future time — as a genuine alternative to jumping into Teams or Zoom. To actually launch one, you first search for the candidate — typically by first and last name, though email, phone, city, state, or zip all work too — and once you've found them, a Schedule a Live Interview window opens with the subject line already filled in, something like Video Interview with Steve Smith. From there you choose Now if you want to jump straight into the call, or pick a specific future date and time instead, and JobDiva automatically rewrites the subject line to match whichever option you select. The message box comes pre-populated with instructions telling the candidate to use an up-to-date browser with a working camera and microphone, along with a clickable join link and a fallback URL they can paste into their browser if the link doesn't cooperate. You can edit that message freely before sending — add your own note, adjust the tone, whatever fits — and clicking Send fires it off immediately. Every interview you conduct or schedule gets logged under My Recorded Live Interviews, searchable by candidate name, email, or date range. It's a genuinely lightweight way to get a candidate in front of a camera fast, especially compared to setting up a separate meeting link through Teams or Zoom and hoping the candidate finds it in their inbox in time. Give the candidate a minute after you send that link before assuming something's wrong — email delivery and a candidate actually noticing and clicking it aren't always instant, especially for a same-day invite.

E-Interviews work differently: they're a pre-built set of questions a candidate fills out asynchronously, on their own schedule, using text, multiple choice, audio, or even video answers, either before a live interview or sometimes instead of one entirely. The My e-interviews screen is your home base for this feature — it lists every e-interview you've assigned, along with the candidate's name, the date it was assigned, its current status, and a score column once results come in. You can search past assignments by candidate first or last name, by e-interview name, or by a date range, which is handy once you've sent out more than a handful. In the top right, e-interview Settings lets you manage your library of question sets, while Assign New e-interview opens the builder where you configure everything about the questionnaire itself, starting with its name, an expiration window, and how you'll score responses once they come back. Think of this list the way you'd think of My Jobs Dashboard — it's the one screen where you can see the current state of every e-interview you've sent out, without having to remember who you assigned what to.

Here's an important detail behind the video-answer option specifically: requiring a video response helps authenticate that the real candidate is the one actually answering, which matters because this is used deliberately in IT recruiting to catch proxy or forgery candidates — cases where someone other than the actual applicant tries to interview in their place. To send an e-interview, you build the questionnaire first, naming it, setting an expiration date, and defining each question's time limit and answer format. Each question gets its own dedicated screen: you type the question text into a box, set an optional time limit in minutes and seconds so candidates can't stall indefinitely, and then pick exactly how they'll answer — Single Select and Multi Select for multiple-choice style questions, Written Answer for free-text responses, Record an Audio Answer, or Record a Video Answer for that authentication-friendly option we just talked about. A live preview panel on the right shows exactly what the candidate will see, time limit and all, and there's a separate box for internal scoring instructions that only your team sees, never the candidate. Once a question is set up the way you want, Save and Add More takes you straight into building the next one, so you can stack up as many questions as the role needs before finishing with Save and Quit. For instance, one LPN-focused set includes a straightforward written question — how much experience do you have in hospital? — with a three-minute, four-second time limit, showing just how granular that per-question timing control really is. That per-question flexibility is really the point of building your own set instead of reusing a generic one — a technical role might need every answer on video for authentication, while a straightforward screening question is often just as effective as plain text.

You're not limited to building from scratch every time, either — once you've created a set like this MS Power Platform Developer questionnaire, it's saved and reusable, and you can open any of its six questions from the tabs across the top to review or edit them later. Each question keeps its own preview, including a placeholder for a recorded video answer where a real submission would eventually appear, and a delete option in the sidebar if a question no longer fits what you're screening for. That reusability is really the point: build a strong technical question bank once, for a role like this, and you can assign it to candidate after candidate without rebuilding it every time. It's a good habit to build toward — a well-organized, reusable set like this one saves real time across every requisition for that role. And because every question already has its format, timing, and scoring notes locked in, all you're really doing on reuse is picking the candidate and hitting send. That's exactly the kind of setup work that pays for itself the second or third time you assign it — the harder job is building the set well once, not reusing it afterward, which takes only seconds and a couple of clicks.

Then you look up the candidate and click Assign — which, like the other Engagement tools, immediately emails them the invitation. Once you've looked up the candidate, a picker shows every e-interview you've built — LPN Questions, MS Power Platform Developer, RN Questions — along with how many questions each contains, so you can match the right set to the role. Clicking the Send e-interview icon fires off the invitation immediately, and you land back on the My e-interviews list, where that assignment will show its status and score once completed.

5.1.text: We now arrive at Talent Search — genuinely the single most-used tool in a recruiter's day, accounting for an estimated eighty percent of daily work. It's worth slowing down here, because everything else in your sourcing workflow builds on what you learn in this module. You'll find Talent Search under the Sourcing section of your apps menu, right alongside New Candidate, Search Candidates, Search Employees, Candidate Hotlists, and a few other sourcing tools — it's worth exploring that whole row at some point, but Talent Search is where you'll live day to day. Once you open it, you're dropped into a search form built around several tabs across the top: Profession/Specialty, Licenses, Certifications, Qualification, Require, Exclude, Attribute, and Title. Each tab lets you narrow the candidate pool from a different angle — Profession/Specialty, for instance, gives you a long list of pre-built categories like RN, CNA, LPN LVN, Nurse Practitioner, Physician Assistant, Mammography Technologist, Social Work, and Therapy, each with its own ADD button so you can stack several categories into a single search. Below the tabs you'll also find practical filters that apply no matter which search style you're using: a date field for candidates available on or prior to a certain day, checkboxes for real-time access to outside job boards like Dice and Monster, an option to restrict results to just what's already in JobDiva, and sorting controls for sequencing what comes back. It's a genuinely dense screen the first time you see it, but you'll come back to the same handful of tabs constantly, so the layout becomes second nature fast. And once you've made your picks across however many tabs you need, a single Search click pulls together everyone who matches, which is the moment we'll pick up with next. Don't worry about memorizing every tab right now — in practice, most searches only ever touch two or three of them, and we're about to walk through exactly which ones matter most and why, starting with the two you'll use constantly: Title and Boolean search.

Talent Search offers two fundamentally different approaches. Title Search looks for an exact job title match, like R-N or L-P-N, and returns a narrow, highly specific pool of candidates whose titles literally say that. On the Title tab, you type a title into the Titles field — say 'REG' — and JobDiva suggests matches like Registered Nurse. An 'Alternate' button then lets you stack on OR variations, so you might end up with Registered Nurse, RN, and LPN all chained together into one query: titles equals Registered Nurse or RN or LPN. Each row also carries Years, Recent, and w-slash-o Mapping checkboxes, letting you require minimum experience in that title or search for titles that haven't been mapped yet. It's a fast way to cover several equivalent job titles without leaving the same search tab.

Boolean Search, by contrast, is built from logical operators and returns a much broader set of results, including variations, synonyms, and related terms you might not have thought to type yourself. Neither approach is universally better — they're tools for different moments. Choose Title Search when you want a small, precise pool and you already know exactly what you're looking for. Choose Boolean Search when you want to expand your reach, combine multiple criteria, or you're not entirely sure which exact title a strong candidate might be using on their own resume.

5.2.text: Boolean search is built from six operators, and mastering them is genuinely foundational to everything else you'll do in Talent Search. AND requires both keywords to be present at the same time — RN AND ICU means a candidate needs both. OR returns results containing either keyword, which is especially useful for capturing title variations, like ICU OR Emergency Room.

AND NOT includes the first keyword while explicitly excluding the second, letting you narrow a pool that's technically correct but too broad. Quotation marks force an exact multi-word phrase match — "registered nurse" as a phrase — and a rule worth remembering: quotation marks are never used around a single word, only genuine multi-word phrases.

Parenthesis groups keywords together to control the logic and order of your search, and without it, a multi-part Boolean string becomes genuinely meaningless to the system — it simply can't parse what you intended.

And finally, the asterisk, or wildcard, matches keyword variations, so manage-asterisk would catch managed, management, and managing — but here's the catch worth remembering: it is NOT supported inside JobDiva itself. It only works on external boards like Monster, Dice, or CareerBuilder. Building a genuinely strong Boolean string is a skill that improves with practice and real domain knowledge — there's no single fixed formula that works for every search.

5.3.text: Let's build a search from scratch on the Talent Search screen, starting with the Title tab. Type in a title — Registered Nurse, for example — and if there's a common abbreviation, like RN, add it as an alternate so both terms get captured together. The w/o Mapping checkbox lets you require an exact title match instead of JobDiva's automatic title mapping, which comes in handy when you need precision rather than a broad match. Right next to it, the years field lets you require a minimum number of years in that title, so you can narrow your pool by seniority as you build out the rest of the search. Notice the New Title button just below — that's how you add a second or third title, each one OR'd together automatically, so you're not limited to a single job title per search. The Recent checkbox is worth flagging too: checking it restricts results to candidates whose title was updated recently in their profile, a quick way to filter out stale records. And once your title logic is dialed in, glance at the live string preview at the bottom of the screen — it updates instantly as you check boxes and add alternates, so you can confirm the logic is exactly what you intended before moving on to layer in more criteria. That habit alone will save you from chasing down mismatched search results later. That live string preview is worth checking after every single change you make here, not just at the end — catching a logic mistake while it's still one click away beats catching it after you've already run the search.

Switch over to the Require tab, and you'll see Boolean Search working in real time: as you add keywords like Registered Nurse, RN, ICU, and Intensive Care Unit — grouping the title terms with OR and joining that group to the unit terms with AND — JobDiva builds the actual Boolean string for you at the bottom of the screen, so you never have to hand-type the parentheses and operators yourself. Now head over to Profession and Specialty. Instead of typing out every specialty term by hand, just click Add next to a preloaded specialty like RN, and a list of specific unit types appears — Burn ICU, Cardiac Care, Case Management, and dozens more. Selecting one, like Burn ICU here, narrows an otherwise broad pool of RNs down to exactly the specialty population you're recruiting for, instead of manually typing every specialty term yourself. Notice too that you're not limited to one specialty at a time — each one you add here gets OR'd into the search automatically, so selecting Burn ICU alongside, say, Cardiac Care widens your pool to either specialty without you touching the Boolean string directly. If a specialty falls out of scope later, just hit Remove next to it and JobDiva instantly rewrites the underlying search string to match, so you're always working from a clean, accurate query. Take a second look at that live preview after adding each specialty, too — it's the fastest way to confirm JobDiva grouped your OR logic exactly the way you expected, before you've layered on anything else.

Scroll down to the bottom of the screen for a moment, because this next section controls where your search actually reaches. You'll see checkboxes for Real Time Job Board Access alongside the specific boards JobDiva has integrated for your account — toggle Real Time off and on here to see how the available board options change, and check Only Include Results in JobDiva if you want to restrict things strictly to candidates already sitting in your own database rather than pulling in fresh board listings. Once you click Search, JobDiva paginates the results — you can see here it's returning well over a hundred matches, and you can page through fifty at a time, sorting or scanning column by column, to start narrowing down who's worth a closer look. Get comfortable toggling that Real Time checkbox on and off a few times before you commit — watching how the available board list changes each time is the fastest way to understand exactly what each option is actually doing.

Now let's talk about where these candidates actually come from. Real Time Job Board Access, down here, searches live across every job board assigned to your account. If you'd rather narrow to one specific board — Monster, in this case — uncheck real-time access and select it directly, and you'll unlock board-specific sort and filter options: relevancy, resume-updated date, or last-active date, depending on what matters most for that search. With Only Include Results in JobDiva checked as well, running the search pulls back everything that matches, ready for you to review, qualify, or add straight to a hot list. Once results come back, take a moment to get familiar with this results grid, because you'll live in it constantly. The little icons in the e and B columns let you exclude a candidate from this particular search or flag them for a Hotlist with a single click, right from the list, without opening their profile first. The Qualify button works the same way — select one or more rows with the checkboxes on the left, then click Qualify to mark them as vetted for this requirement, which keeps your team from duplicating screening work on the same person. Preview gives you a quick summary card without leaving the page, while Expand opens a fuller view showing experience, availability, and submission history side by side, which is handy when you're comparing several similar candidates at once. Notice the pagination controls at the bottom too — with over a hundred results here, you can bump the page size up from fifty to a hundred at a time, or just click Next repeatedly, and the Received and Available date columns let you sort so the freshest resumes surface first. All of this happens without ever leaving the results screen, which is really the point: JobDiva keeps sourcing, qualifying, and shortlisting in one continuous flow instead of forcing you to bounce between separate tools. Now, let's go back to the search screen itself, because there's more criteria worth layering on before we wrap up this lesson, since a lighter, well-targeted string usually beats a heavily filtered one. It's worth spending your first few searches just clicking through Preview and Expand on a handful of candidates, even ones you don't end up qualifying, purely to get a feel for how much detail each view actually gives you — that upfront orientation pays off every time afterward, when you're moving fast through a genuinely large results page like this one. Give the page a moment to fully load before you start clicking Preview or Expand on individual rows — with a results set this size, jumping in too early sometimes means paging back to where you started.

Back on the search screen, you can keep layering on criteria: a state like Florida, or a zip code with an exact-match or within-a-radius option, under Location; a degree requirement under Education; specific licenses and certifications, each with its own expiration and documentation requirements, under the Certifications tab; and qualification-based filters, like Wallet Status, under Qualification. But here's the guiding principle to keep in mind through all of this: the lighter the string, the more results you'll get. Specialty and title alone usually deliver strong outcomes on their own — stacking on every available filter tends to shrink your candidate pool far more than it helps narrow it meaningfully. There's also an Exclude tab, which technically maps to AND NOT logic — watch how adding LPN here appends 'but not equals LPN' to the string — but in practice it's often unnecessary once your search criteria is already clearly defined. Let's take a closer look at a few of these tabs before we close out. Open the Certifications dropdown and you'll see just how many are tracked in JobDiva — ACLS, AHA ACLS, AHA BLS, BLS, CCRN, CEN, CNOR, Color Vision, Competency Exam Specialty, several Core Mandatory Part levels, COVID, and many more scroll past that. For each one you select, you can set an Expiring After date, so you only surface candidates whose certification is still valid going forward, and you can check Require Documentation if you need proof on file rather than a self-reported credential. Over on the Qualification tab, Wallet Status breaks candidates into Complete, Expired, or Incomplete — Complete means every required document and screening step is already on file, which is exactly why it's worth adding here when you need candidates who are truly ready to submit today, not ones still working through onboarding paperwork. If you jump back to Profession and Specialty, notice you can always add a second or third specialty alongside Burn ICU the same way we did earlier, and each addition only makes the pool broader, never narrower, since they're OR'd together. Now, over on the Exclude tab — type LPN into the keyword field here and watch the string preview update at the bottom in real time, appending exactly 'AND NOT LPN' to whatever you've already built. It's a clean way to rule out a title you know will otherwise slip through your Boolean logic. To wrap up this lesson: start light, with just title and specialty, run the search, and only add tabs like Location, Certifications, or Exclude if your first pass is genuinely too broad. Adding filters is easy — undoing an overly narrow search and starting over costs you far more time. Keep it simple, and JobDiva does the heavy lifting.

5.4.text: Now it's your turn. Using everything you've learned so far — AND, OR, AND NOT, quotation marks, and parentheses — construct a Boolean string for this exact requirement: a registered nurse for a burn intensive care unit, with hospital experience required, needing both ACLS and BLS certification. Take a genuine moment to pause here and write your string out before moving on. Think through it piece by piece: which terms need OR to capture title variations, which need AND to require multiple things at once, and — critically — where the parentheses need to go to group those clauses correctly so the whole string actually parses the way you intend. Once you've written your version, compare it against the model answer described in the lesson notes, and pay particular attention to whether your parenthesis placement matches the intended logic. This is the exact live exercise given to trainees in the original session — treat it as a genuine checkpoint before moving forward, not something to skip past. Take the extra time here if you need it — there's no rush, and building this instinct now will save you real time on live searches later. If you find yourself stuck, go back to the specialty and title logic we walked through in the previous lesson and rebuild your string piece by piece rather than trying to write the whole thing at once. Getting comfortable with this pattern is genuinely the difference between a search that returns exactly who you're looking for and one that returns almost nothing at all.

6.1.text: There are four distinct ways to add a new candidate to JobDiva, and it's worth knowing all four since different situations call for different ones. Let's start with Upload: select a resume file directly from your computer — just keep it under five megabytes — and once JobDiva processes it, you'll land on a verification page. Take a moment here to check the auto-extracted Personal Info, Professional Specialty, and Work Experience sections before submitting, since automated parsing isn't always perfect. Scroll down a bit further on this same verification page and you'll find JobDiva's built-in Suggestions feature, which is genuinely useful for catching what the parser missed. If an address wasn't picked up, you'll see a note explaining that city and state matter because they help recruiters judge geographic fit for a role — worth going back and adding manually if it's missing.
