If no work experience was detected at all, JobDiva flags that too, and unless you're dealing with an actual recent graduate applying for a first job, treat that warning seriously and add the missing history yourself using the Insert Experience button, because work history is arguably the single most important section on the whole record. The same logic applies to Education — if nothing was extracted there, you'll get a similar suggestion, and while a missing degree isn't always a dealbreaker, plenty of roles do require one, so it's worth double-checking before you move on. You'll also notice a Profession and Specialty block on this page with Sector, Profession, and Specialty fields — these drive a lot of the search and matching logic we covered in earlier lessons, so it's worth confirming they're accurate here rather than fixing them later. Only once you're satisfied that personal info, profession and specialty, work experience, and education all look right should you click Submit at the bottom. It might feel slower to check every section, but a few extra seconds here saves you from submitting a candidate with a broken or misleading profile down the line. None of these checks take long once you know to look for them — it's really a ten-second scroll down the same page you're already on — but skipping that scroll entirely is exactly how an incomplete or mis-parsed candidate record slips into your database, only to cause confusion for whoever pulls it up in a search weeks later. Give yourself permission to slow down on this very first candidate you add, even if it feels tedious — the goal isn't speed on record one, it's building the checking habit so it becomes automatic by record twenty.

Dedicated email upload works differently: you simply email the resume to a dedicated address — right here, honorvettech@jobdivaemail.com — and you'll get a confirmation once it's been added to the system, no manual data entry required on your end.
Copy-paste lets you select a source, or none at all, and paste the full resume text directly into this field before clicking Submit.

And manual entry — Register Without Resume — lets you add just a few key details and save, creating a bare candidate record when you don't have a full resume in hand. One field deserves special attention here: the Professional Specialty section is explicitly called out as very important, specifically for healthcare resumes, so don't skip it even when you're moving quickly. And regardless of which method you use, always verify the auto-extracted fields before clicking Submit — never trust automated parsing blindly.

6.2.text: To find an existing candidate rather than add a new one, Lookup a Candidate works fastest when you have a name, email, and phone number together — the more of these three you can provide, like we're doing here with Tyler Connally's name and phone number, the more precisely JobDiva narrows the match. Notice you can also expand the Profession/Specialty section right here on the Lookup screen — selecting a profession like CNA immediately surfaces a checklist of related specialties such as Acute, Clinic, or Home Health, letting you narrow an already-precise name-and-phone lookup even further whenever there happen to be multiple close matches to sort through.

Search Candidate takes a slightly different approach, letting you filter by contact info or by professional specialty and profession, which is useful when you're browsing rather than looking for one specific person. There's also an important distinction worth understanding clearly, right alongside Search Candidates here: an employee — found through Search Employees — is someone who's already been placed, while a candidate is still somewhere in sourcing or submittal, not yet working. That status only changes from candidate to employee after a very specific sequence: an interview happens, the candidate accepts, the client confirms onboarding, and finally a Start is formally recorded inside JobDiva. Nobody manually types 'employee' anywhere — it's a system consequence of that Start being properly recorded, which we'll cover in much more depth later in this course when we walk through the full HireTrack process. Before we move on, it's worth taking a quick look at the App Menu, since it ties together everything we've covered about finding candidates and employees so far. Under the Sourcing section here, you'll find Talent Search and New Candidate on the left, then Search Candidates and Search Employees right next to each other — a visual reminder of that exact distinction we just walked through. Candidate Hotlists sits right alongside them, which is where those saved searches we'll build in an upcoming lesson live permanently. Search Candidate Notes lets you look up any notes ever logged against a candidate, Search Attributes lets you query on custom fields your organization has configured, and Import Candidates is there for bulk-loading records rather than adding them one at a time. Clicking into any existing candidate, like this record here, drops you straight into their full profile — resume view, activity history, qualifications, licenses, and experience all live down the left-hand side, with tabs across the top for things like Candidate Wallet, DivaMatch, Onboard, and Live Interviews. That's the same profile view you'll land in no matter which of the lookup or search methods got you there, so once you're comfortable with Lookup, Search Candidate, and Search Employee, you're really just choosing the fastest door into this same destination. Take a minute now to explore this menu on your own before we move into building hot lists in the next lesson, where we'll turn a saved search into something that works for you automatically.

6.3.text: A Hot List is your personal, curated list of favorite candidates for a specific role — and it does more than just save your picks, since it also automatically fetches new matching resumes based on a saved search string you define once and let run in the background. You'll find Hot Lists from the App Menu, under Sourcing, right alongside Candidate Hotlists. Once you're in, notice there are two tabs: Search Hotlists shows every hot list across the whole organization — you can see names like Andy, Gunjan, Navneet Kaur, and dozens of others here, each tied to a Job Ref number, a note, and the user who owns it — while My Hotlists narrows that same view down to just the ones you personally created or were assigned to, which in this example is only two: Andy and TTT. That distinction matters day to day: Search Hotlists is how you find a colleague's hot list when you need to collaborate or hand off a role, while My Hotlists is your own personal workspace, the one you'll open constantly once you're actively sourcing for a role. Either way, everything you see in both tabs lives in the same underlying system — nothing here is siloed away per individual recruiter. It's a small distinction, but a genuinely useful one to internalize early: reach for Search Hotlists when you're trying to find something that already exists somewhere in the organization, and reach for My Hotlists when you're building or maintaining your own active pipeline.

To build one, click New Hot List, define your search criteria using Boolean logic plus specialty and state — here we're combining Registered Nurse or RN with Burn ICU, narrowed down to New Jersey — then name that saved string clearly, like Komal, and link it to the relevant job before saving. One important boundary to remember: never assign users, groups, or divisions to a hot list yourself — that's reserved specifically for managers. On the setup screen itself, give the hot list a clear Name and a short Description — RN, in this case — then use Link to Job to tie it to the specific requisition, like this Correctional RN posting, Ref number 26-20036. There's also a handy checkbox, Include all non-rejected Applicants to this Job in Hotlist, which auto-populates the list with everyone still active in your pipeline for that role instead of making you add each person one at a time. Below that, Add Users, Add Groups, and Add Divisions give you long checklists — individual recruiters, teams like Business Development or specific Healthcare groups, and divisions like Clinical, IT, or Recruiting — but remember, populating those is a manager's call, not yours. Once the name, description, and job link are set, click Save, and your hot list is live and ready to start collecting candidates. That's the whole setup, quick and repeatable every time. Get in the habit of naming your hot lists something a colleague could recognize at a glance too, not just something that makes sense to you in the moment.

Once your hot list exists, adding a favorite candidate is as simple as clicking its dedicated icon from the candidate's profile, then refreshing to confirm it stuck — notice how Charles Lewis now shows up right here in the list. Removing works the same way, either from the hot list itself or from the candidate's own profile page. Two viewing options round this out, right at the top: Preview shows a short candidate summary inline without leaving the page, while Expand shows considerably more detail, including how a candidate's actual years of experience stack up against what your saved criteria requires. There's actually a cleaner way to manage this from the candidate's own profile too: open their record, and you'll find a small hotlist icon that opens a Manage Hotlists window showing every list that candidate currently belongs to, each with its own X to remove them instantly. It even offers a Create a New Candidate Hotlist link right there, so you're never forced to leave the profile just to start a brand-new list around someone you just found. Next, we'll put this exact same logic to work managing candidates at scale in HireTrack.

6.4.text: Search Candidate Notes filters by note content, action, and date, but works best with standardized actions like RTR Log, rather than informal shorthand like 'logged' or 'DNC.'

Attributes capture submittal-required details, like the last four digits of the candidate's Social Security Number and their date of birth, tied directly to the quality-audit process. These fields must be filled in for every submission, or the submission won't pass audit.

7.1.text: When you have many resumes to add at once rather than one at a time, use Bulk Upload instead of the standard New Candidate flow. Select your source first, optionally link the entire batch to a hot list right from the same screen — which saves you a separate step later — and then upload, keeping in mind the hard limit of fewer than fifty files per single batch. On the Bulk Upload screen itself, you'll see a Resume Source dropdown — leave it on the appropriate source, or choose Other when nothing else fits — right above the optional Select a Hotlist field, where typing a few letters pulls up matching hotlists so you can attach the whole batch to one, like tagging every resume you're about to import for a specific client or campaign in a single step. Click Add Files to open your computer's file browser, navigate to wherever the resumes are stored — your Desktop, a shared drive, a folder a client or vendor sent over — and select as many files as you need, up to that fifty-file limit. Each file then lands in the Filename list below with its size shown in kilobytes and a Status column starting at zero percent, so you can double-check you've grabbed the right documents, in the right combination, before committing to anything. Only once everything looks correct do you click Start Upload, and JobDiva's parsing robot takes it from there, reading each resume and building out a full candidate record automatically, without you lifting a finger. Once you click Start Upload, resist the urge to immediately move on to something else — give the Status column a moment to climb toward completion first, since a batch that stalls partway through, especially a large one, is much easier to catch and retry right away than to notice hours later.

This is genuinely one of the biggest time-savers available when you're processing a large stack of resumes from a career fair, a referral drive, or a bulk email from a vendor, since doing them one at a time would take far longer for the same result.

7.2.text: The Job toolbar includes two handy shortcuts worth knowing: Clone, which duplicates an existing job under a brand-new JobDiva ID — useful when a client reopens a nearly identical position — and Merge, which combines two job records and lets you choose which details from each to keep. When you click Merge, JobDiva opens a Merge Job window listing your open jobs that share a common contact with the one you're merging — check the box for 'Include my jobs that are not open' if the job you need is already closed — then click Continue to step through and choose exactly which fields, like requirements or candidates, carry over from each record before finalizing the merge. Take a second to confirm which of the two records is actually the live one afterward, too — a cloned job and its original can otherwise look confusingly similar in a shared job list until you check the JobDiva ID.

Before covering the LinkedIn-specific rules, notice the Post to Job Boards window itself: it's organized into tabs for Other, Monster, Resume-Library, LinkedIn, and Dice, alongside options like showing the pay rate on your candidate portal, the posting date, and the portal job category, plus a reminder to fill in City, State, Zip, Job Title, and a two-hundred-character Job Description first.

When it comes to posting a job to LinkedIn, remember this firm sequence, because it trips people up constantly: the job must be Open, Assigned, and Saved before the LinkedIn posting fields even appear on screen.

And keep in mind that company-portal and Monster or Dice posting from directly within JobDiva depends on whether integration slots are available for your account; otherwise, you'll post directly on those platforms instead. On this same Post to Job Boards screen, each destination — like your own company portal — shows its own row with a website name, username, posting limit, and current status, so you can see at a glance whether a listing is already Posted or still waiting to go out.

LinkedIn posting always uses your company's integrated account, never a personal one — you'll set the contract ID, degree, industry, employment status, and expiry date, then post. Expect a short backend delay before it actually goes live, so don't assume something failed if it's not instant. The LinkedIn tab shows a Current LinkedIn Job Status section confirming whether the listing is live, plus Post/Update, Renew, and Delete Post buttons to manage it.

7.3.text: Job Applicants shows everyone who applied through an integrated portal or directly through your company website, all funneled into one place; accepting an applicant automatically creates their candidate profile for you, no manual entry required. If a job hasn't drawn any applicants yet, opening this same list simply shows 'No Candidates have applied for this Job,' a quick way to confirm whether your posting is actually live and gaining traction.

Email Job lets you send the position directly to a candidate by email — but always confirm the right template with your manager first rather than defaulting to whatever's preloaded, since templates are often client- or role-specific and using the wrong one can send mixed signals. The Message field auto-populates with the job's key details pulled straight from the record — job number, title, location, whether travel or overtime is required, and the entire job description below that, including things like patient age groups, diagnoses, and staffing ratios for a healthcare role like this one — so you can review it, trim anything overly detailed, or highlight and edit specific sections before you hit Send.

And Email Merge tracking shows you, per job, exactly who received your outreach, whether they actually opened it, and what action followed afterward — giving you a real feedback loop on how effective your outreach has been, rather than just sending emails into the void.

7.4.text: Harvest is JobDiva's automated sourcing engine — once you activate it on a saved search string, it continuously feeds matching resumes from the internal database straight into an active job, working in the background even while you're focused on something else.

Toggle it on or off using Schedule and Not Schedule, and always remember to click Save afterward; the toggle genuinely has no effect until you do — a lot of recruiters assume it's active the moment they flip the switch, and it simply isn't. This same Agent Search panel is also where the actual search string lives — you can see it rendered at the bottom as, for example, quotation-marked keywords in parentheses, built automatically from whatever you type into the Keywords box up top. You can stack multiple keywords together with the OR button, add a brand-new skill line entirely with New Skill, and narrow further using State, Area Codes, Zip Code, Pay Range, and Major over on the right, plus a 'Display candidates available on or prior to' date filter and a Real Time Job Board Access checkbox that determines whether Harvest pulls live from job boards or sticks to what's already inside JobDiva. None of this needs to be perfect on the first try — you can always come back and adjust the string later, and Harvest will simply pick up the change on its next scheduled run. It's worth taking a moment to get this right, since Harvest will keep running against whatever criteria you save here for as long as the job stays active. It's worth revisiting this string every so often rather than treating it as set-and-forget — a role's core requirements rarely change, but the exact skills or keywords worth searching for often do, especially as a client's needs evolve over the life of a long-running requisition.

Clicking further into the criteria also opens an Edit Job Board Criteria window, letting you edit Required Skills and Years Recent directly, tighten things by State or Zip Code, and hit Save — a faster path than rebuilding the whole search from scratch.

There's also an AI feature that can suggest a search-criteria string based on the job description itself, which is a great starting point if you're not sure where to begin building your own string. Once generated, it populates the Agent Search fields directly — in this example, pairing 'REGISTERED NURSE' or RN with a two-year recency requirement, then chaining in BLS or Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation, ONS Chemo, and EPIC with AND logic — and it even sets Harvest to run immediately, pulling in a batch of new candidates right away rather than waiting for the next scheduled pass.

Beyond Harvest, you can also post a job to a staffing network like Vivian, right from the User Fields tab: select the network, set Post on Vivian to yes, add the travel or weekly rate along with any shift information, and save. Expect roughly thirty to forty-five minutes before it actually reflects live, so don't panic if it's not there instantly. Notice too that User Fields covers more than Vivian — tabs for Healthcare, IT, Wanderly, Others, and Change Management sit alongside it, plus a blank Shift box to spell out details before clicking Save.

8.1.text: The Activities section logs every submission, interview update, and Start performed by any team member on a given job — you can see those Submitted, Interviewed, and Started counts right here on the job order. That makes it genuinely worth checking before you submit a candidate yourself, simply to avoid duplicating a colleague's work on the exact same position. You can even log a new activity directly from here, like we're doing now, to record exactly what happened and when. That said, the trainer specifically recommends performing your actual submissions from the candidate's own profile rather than directly from Activities, since that path carries more of the relevant candidate context along with it automatically — their resume, their notes, their contact history are all right there with them, instead of buried in a shared activity log that everyone on the team is touching.

Before any of that shows up as results, this is Agent Search — the actual screen where you build the query. Stack keyword groups with AND and OR logic, layer in required years of experience, and JobDiva assembles the full boolean string for you right here in this preview box as you go.

Once you run that search, this is the Search Criteria page — it shows every resume matching your applied criteria in real time, and it keeps updating as new matches come into the system, so the list you're looking at is never stale. You can see each candidate's name, phone number, city and state, when their resume was received, when they're available, and any last note or last submittal on file, all in one sortable table — here alone we're already looking at over a hundred matching candidates for this single search. When you just need a fast read on someone, use the Preview option for a quick inline summary without ever leaving this list, so you can keep moving down the results instead of clicking in and out of full profiles one at a time.

Watch what happens next: the trainer strips this search back down to a single broad keyword, 'Registered Nurse,' and reruns it — pulling out those AND conditions for BLS, ONS Chemo, and EPIC immediately opens the pool up, since each requirement had been narrowing the results. That's a useful troubleshooting habit: if a compound search comes back too thin, loosen it one filter at a time, rerun, and see how much each requirement was costing you in matching candidates. Here the broader search pulls back well over a hundred results, and from this same screen the trainer pages into a fuller view to browse that larger pool before deciding which filters are worth adding back. That same instinct — loosen one filter at a time and watch what comes back — is worth applying anywhere in JobDiva a search feels too narrow, not just here in Talent Search or Agent Search.

When a quick preview isn't enough, Expand gives you a considerably more detailed, full view of the results — exactly what you'd reach for when you need real depth on a specific candidate before deciding whether to move them forward for this job. From here you can page through the entire matching pool, fifty candidates at a time, scanning resumes, contact details, and availability as you go, rather than being limited to a short list. Notice, too, that Bulk Text and Email Merge sit right on this same results screen, letting you reach out to a large batch of these matching candidates at once instead of contacting them one by one — that's a genuine time-saver when you're staring down a pool this size, and it's exactly what we're going to walk through in detail next, in the section on Email Merge. Before we move into Email Merge, notice you can also sort this expanded list by any column — Received, Available, Last Submittal — to surface the freshest, most promising candidates first instead of scrolling straight down an unsorted page of two hundred sixty-eight names one by one. That small habit is exactly what separates a recruiter working efficiently through a large pool from one just scrolling and hoping.

8.2.text: Email Merge lets you reach many candidates at once with a single templated message — a genuinely powerful way to accelerate sourcing when you have a large qualified pool, like the list of matches we just pulled, and limited time to call everyone individually. The first step is simple: confirm that this candidate list in front of you is actually the right group before you commit to messaging all of them, since Email Merge is going to act on the search results you've already built. Scroll through and scan a handful of names before you commit — it only takes a second, and it's far easier to catch a stray unrelated candidate now than to explain an off-target email after it's already been sent.

From here, the workflow is: select a sender email and a template, choose your batch size, and optionally skip candidates you've already contacted for similar roles — you can see all three of those choices laid out right in this dialog, along with checkboxes to skip current employees, anyone already text-merged, or anyone who's already gotten an email merge on these jobs. Notice the template dropdown defaults to a saved Healthcare_Template here, and you can also limit the send to candidates available on or before a specific date, so you're not emailing people whose availability window has already passed. Here's the critical guidance to actually remember: keep each batch at or under roughly three hundred recipients. Going bigger risks your email getting flagged as spam, and it can genuinely draw scrutiny from your own IT team over unusual outbound volume from your account. Take a second look at those checkboxes before you click Next — once you've confirmed the sender, the template, and who gets skipped, you're ready to move into actually shaping the message itself. Take a moment before you finalize that batch size to actually picture who's on the other end of each message — a well-targeted smaller send usually outperforms a larger, less-qualified one anyway.

Before you send, it's worth 'beautifying' the template — adding job description highlights, urgent-hiring framing, and location details, the way this Subject line dropdown is doing right here, pulling in the exact job title and address so the message reads as specific and urgent rather than generic. Use either an IT- or healthcare-specific template already saved to the job, or one your manager provides, then add your signature and hit Send Emails. And always check for, and honor, any candidate's specific request to be excluded from future mass outreach — that's not optional courtesy, it's a compliance expectation. Once you hit Send, JobDiva takes you right back to your results list so you can pick up where you left off, and every one of these sends gets logged automatically on each candidate's own Email and Text Merge History, so nobody on your team accidentally messages the same person twice.

8.3.text: A candidate's Availability status is visible to every recruiter who shares access to that candidate — right now you can see it flagged directly under this candidate's name, 'Unavailable Until 08/07/2026,' in red so it's impossible to miss. When you open the Change Availability screen, like we're doing here for a different candidate, you've got four real options: Available as of a specific date, Available Now, Unavailable Indefinitely, or Unavailable Until a date you set — and in every case, you can add a note explaining why, which gets saved right along with the status. That shared visibility is genuinely valuable, because it prevents multiple recruiters on your team from redundantly calling someone who has already told you no, or who's already out on an assignment and unavailable. Think about how often a healthcare candidate goes on assignment for months at a time — if that isn't reflected here, you or a teammate could spend real time chasing someone who was never going to answer. Setting this status the moment you learn it takes a few seconds and saves everyone downstream a wasted phone call.

Here we've clicked into another candidate's profile, Michelle Williams, to walk through that same workflow end to end. Opening her Availability screen shows the opt-out and opt-in controls sitting right inside this same panel — alongside the four availability options and the email-merge checkboxes — so setting when someone's available and controlling whether they receive email merges both happen from one screen instead of two. Notice, too, that a candidate's profile carries a running Notes count and an 'Add to hotlist' option right in the sidebar, which is exactly where you'd log why an availability change was made, or flag someone you want to circle back to later. That kind of detail, logged consistently, is what keeps a shared candidate record useful to the whole team, not just to whoever last touched it. Notice how much of this — availability, opt-out status, notes — lives in one consolidated panel rather than scattered across separate tabs, which is exactly what makes a quick check like this fast enough to do before every single outreach.

The opt-out link lets a candidate stop receiving emails entirely — right here you've got a 'Generate Opt-Out Link' button and a matching 'Send Opt-In Email' button in the exact same panel, so if someone opts out and later changes their mind, you're not stuck; you can send them a link that lets them opt back into email merges just as easily. Notice the system even double-checks you before that opt-in email goes out, confirming you actually want to send that link to the candidate. The same idea applies to texting — this candidate's Texting Consent Settings show an Opt Out and an Opt In button sitting right next to their phone number, so whichever channel a candidate used to reach out, you have a clean, one-click way to honor a request to stop, and just as clean a way to invite them back in if they ask. This isn't just a nice-to-have — respecting a candidate's stated preference here is part of doing right by the people you're trying to place, and it's tracked and visible so nobody on the team accidentally re-adds someone who's asked to be left alone.

Every email and text merge gets logged here too — this Email and Text Merge History screen lists every message a candidate has ever received, who sent it, which job it went out against, whether it was opened, and how well their resume matched the role at the time. It's worth a quick scroll before you reach out again: a candidate already showing dozens of prior merges against Registered Nurse roles alone is someone you want to message thoughtfully and personally, not just add to the next batch blast without a second thought. That kind of history is exactly what separates a thoughtful, personalized outreach from one that reads as just another mass blast to someone who's already heard from your team a dozen times before.

Do Not Submit works the same protective way, but for a specific client instead of a communication channel: you flag a company or facility this candidate should never be submitted to, pick a documented reason like attendance, behavior, a no-call-no-show, or performance, and save it — though note this feature has to be admin-enabled per user before you can use it yourself. And one firm rule here, learned directly from a real mistake the trainer observed on the team: never, under any circumstances, delete a candidate's resume from the Candidate Information section. It's treated as a serious, entirely avoidable error, and there's simply no good reason to ever do it.

8.4.text: Before we get into rates, notice the References tab on this candidate profile — this is where you log a professional reference's name, job title, company, every phone number you might need, and their full address, along with a Date Checked field so the whole team knows exactly when that reference was actually verified as legitimate. Get in the habit of glancing at Deal History anytime a client mentions a rate that sounds different from what you remember — a quick check here settles the question in seconds, without relying on anyone's memory of a call from months back.

Let's start with rates, since this candidate's Agreed Rates screen is open right in front of us. Every time you and a client settle on a bill rate and pay rate for a candidate, that's the record you want logged here — hit New Rate to add one, and Deal History keeps a running log of exactly how that rate has moved over time, so if a client tries to renegotiate down the road, you've got the actual history to point back to instead of relying on memory. If a client later claims your rate was always higher, Deal History is your evidence — it timestamps every revision, so there's no ambiguity about what was actually agreed and when, no matter how much time has passed.

Licenses, certifications, and qualifications aren't just administrative record-keeping — they directly power your search results down the line. This is the Add License screen, where you can log any of the license types JobDiva tracks, each with its own license number, state, country, and expiration date. Add those details complete with expiration dates, and enable automatic expiration alerts right here — sending them to subscribed users or to the candidate themselves — so people get reminded before something lapses without anyone having to track it manually.

Just as important: always tag a candidate's Profession and Specialty, and fill in their Qualifications — you can see both of those sections right here in the candidate's sidebar, things like work authorization and shift preference live there. Skip these fields, and a filtered search — say, for a specific work-authorization status — will return few or no results, even when perfectly qualified candidates genuinely exist somewhere in your database. This isn't a one-time task; it's long-term team hygiene that compounds into dramatically stronger search results over months and years, which is exactly why the trainer keeps returning to this point throughout the course.

Don't overlook Candidate Social Networks either — this popup lets you attach a candidate's LinkedIn, Facebook, X, YouTube, GitHub, and even a personal professional website directly to their profile, giving you and your team a fuller picture of who you're representing before you ever pick up the phone.

9.1.text: Now we reach the heart of the HireTrack process: ownership and Right to Represent, or R-T-R. This Notes screen is exactly where that gets tracked — you can already see entries here like 'Ownership Taken, Candidate Attached, one week,' sitting right alongside qualification updates from earlier. Before you can claim ownership of a candidate submission, you must first obtain their authorization, either by text message or a signed RTR document, and that order matters enormously.

Claiming ownership without RTR first is a real mistake to actively avoid — it was specifically called out as creating ownership artificially, without the candidate's actual consent ever being given. That's exactly why you see RTR Sent and RTR Received as their own distinct actions right here in this dropdown, each logged with its own note, its own date, and its own time stamp. Log RTR Sent the moment you've asked for authorization, and log RTR Received the moment it actually comes back signed or confirmed by text — that way anyone else on the team who opens this candidate can see at a glance exactly where you are in that process, instead of guessing or, worse, duplicating work you've already started. Notice, too, that you can add a follow-up task for yourself right from this same Notes screen — check the box, set a due date, and JobDiva will remind you automatically instead of leaving it to memory.

The Node section is where you log every action and every conversation status each time you work a candidate — scroll through this Actions list and you'll see the whole lifecycle laid out: Interview Scheduled, Interview Completed, Offer Made, Offer Accepted, Ownership Taken, Ownership Left, and more, so your teammates always know the current state of that relationship before they reach out themselves and risk stepping on each other's outreach. Notice 'Ownership Taken / Candidate Attached' is logged as holding for one week — that's the standard window this process gives you before ownership needs to be reconfirmed. And when it's time for that first real conversation, switch the Templates dropdown to Phone Screening-Healthcare, like we're doing here, and JobDiva drops in a full set of prompts — specialty, licensure, availability, background and compliance questions, and more — so you capture detailed, consistent discussion notes during that initial call instead of relying on memory afterward.

9.2.text: Here's the internal submission workflow, laid out step by step. It starts with pulling up your search results and selecting the assigned job by its JobDiva ID — the specific requisition you're submitting your candidate against.

Once you're in the submittal screen, confirm the position type, then attach the candidate's latest resume from the Resume panel on the right. Choose the manager or Primary Sales contact you're submitting to, then enter the aggregate bill rate and pay rate together so the margin is clear at a glance. Confirm the submission date, time, and time zone — JobDiva fills today's date in for you, but it's worth double-checking that time zone field, since it carries forward into every later interview and start date — and add any internal notes the decision-maker should see before you save. Notice the Corp-to-corp checkbox next to the Agreed Bill Rate — leave it unchecked for a standard placement. Under Notify, decide whether the candidate gets an email too, or just the Primary Sales contact, then click Save to lock everything in.

Once you hit save, JobDiva automatically fires off an email to the decision-maker on the other end. Switch to the healthcare submittal template, like this one, and that email builds out a full clinical profile for you automatically: current title, licensure and compliance details, certifications, and a candidate summary — essentially a background summary at a glance. It also includes an overall suitability rating, from A for best suited down to C for a match, plus a risk flags and concerns section, so you can flag anything the hiring manager should know, honestly and directly. That's exactly the kind of thing that used to take a separate phone call or follow-up email, and now it goes out the moment you click Send. Scroll down a little further and you'll also find a 'What Stands Out' section — quick checkboxes for certification, experience, or interest and motivation. The email even signs off automatically with your own contact details and the HonorVet Technologies letterhead already filled in for you.

And once it's sent, that submission — along with the agreed pay and bill rate — is logged right here under All Activities, tied directly to the job. This single workflow effectively replaces what used to be a manual, back-and-forth request to a manager, and it's especially valuable if you're working remotely, since you're not dependent on catching someone at their desk. One regional note worth knowing: 'cop to cop' rate arrangements are generally not used in healthcare staffing specifically, so don't expect that structure to come up often in this vertical. And if you ever need to revisit it, just click into that logged entry — the same Edit Activity screen opens back up, complete with a Reject This Candidate button if the fit doesn't work out, or a Submit This Candidate Again button if you need to resubmit against a different requisition entirely.

9.3.text: From an internal submission, a manager can either reject the candidate outright or move it forward to external submission with the actual client. Once that happens, you'll come back to this exact same activity screen to update the interview details. And the single most important thing to get exactly right here is the date, time, and time zone together. Confirm all three directly with the hiring manager rather than assuming, because a time-zone mismatch on this screen can cause a candidate to miss an interview entirely, through no fault of their own — so it's worth double-checking that field every single time, even when it feels repetitive. You'll find this interview icon sitting right in the candidate's Activities panel, alongside a whole row of similar quick-action icons for logging every other stage of the process — hover over each one and a tooltip tells you exactly what it does before you click. That extra thirty seconds of double-checking is genuinely worth it every time — a wrong time zone here is invisible until the exact moment the candidate doesn't show up, and by then it's already too late to fix quietly.

The next icon along this row is Start — the action that officially marks a candidate as placed. Recording it opens this same kind of activity screen: job number, hire history, client contact, start date and end date, time zone, start status, and the agreed pay rate. In most organizations, actually clicking Save here is restricted to managers and DMs rather than individual recruiters. Still, it's essential that you understand exactly how this process works end to end, since you'll often be the one gathering every one of these details, even if you're not the one clicking the final button. JobDiva actually protects you here too. Try to record a Start before the candidate's been submitted internally to that job, and an alert stops you cold, reminding you to complete that step first.

Once the start status is set — here, Offer Accepted — and every detail is confirmed, saving this record converts the candidate from a submission into an actual placement, and eventually, an employee on the books. That's why, even if you're not the one pressing this final Save button, knowing exactly what belongs in every field here makes you far more valuable to the manager who is.

9.4.text: A few remaining tools round out the candidate profile. The Wallet aggregates a candidate's certifications, licenses, attachments, and Right to Represent record in one place, saving the whole team repeat verification calls. Resume tools let you upload, download, print, and email a resume, and Find Ideal Job automatically surfaces matching open jobs.

Diva Match, right here, shows a percentage match between a candidate and open jobs — scores like 95, 93, and 92 ranking the best fits at the top, and you can re-sort them by score or by job date. Just always verify a matched job's real status on the client's own portal, though, since JobDiva's status can occasionally lag behind reality.

9.5.text: Let's recap the full journey we've covered in this course. It starts with sourcing through Talent Search using Boolean logic, bringing candidates in through New Candidate intake, and organizing outreach through Hot Lists and Email Merge. Before you ever claim ownership of a candidate, you secure Right to Represent — exactly like this exchange right here, where the candidate replies 'I accept' and grants HonorVet Technologies the exclusive right to submit her resume. From there, it's internal submission, then external submission, careful interview tracking, and finally the Start that completes the placement and turns a candidate into an employee. Notice the rate breakdown baked into that same thread — hourly pay, tax-free stipend, and weekly gross, all spelled out before she ever says yes.

Supporting all of this throughout are tools like the Wallet, resume tools, Diva Match, Notes and Attributes, tasks and live interview scheduling, and Outlook-integrated email tracking — the connective tissue that keeps every step accountable and searchable.

And running underneath the entire course are the healthcare-specific threads worth remembering: Professional Specialty tagging, Submittal Packets, phone screening templates, licenses and compact licenses, and BLS and ACLS certifications.
